docs.title: Tool Registry: Research, Design, and Implementation Plan
docs.text: Context: Inclusive Agentic Architecture — Phase 2 deliverable for Issue #173

docs.title: 1. Problem Statement
docs.text:
The Inclusive Architecture defines a Tool Library used by the Agent Orchestration layer to perform deterministic I/O operations — data retrieval, writes, vector search, object storage, and messaging. The goal is to establish a governed, extensible tool registry that:

  • Is entirely free (no paid SaaS)
  • Gets the foundation right from day one (no "upgrade later" technical debt)
  • Reuses community-maintained MCP servers where they exist
  • Exposes common abstractions for Postgres, MongoDB, Azure Blob, Qdrant, Azure AI Search, LanceDB, and messaging (Azure Queue, Kafka, RabbitMQ)
  • Keeps secrets and credentials completely isolated from the LLM context

docs.title: 2.1 How Leading Companies Approach Tool Registries
docs.text:
Company Approach Key Insight Anthropic MCP Protocol + public MCP Registry (federated) Sub-registries for enterprise private use; tool schema is JSON Schema; tools/list RPC for runtime discovery Microsoft Azure API Center (MCP server catalog) + Semantic Kernel Plugins Plugin = named group of related tool functions; Azure API Center generates OpenAPI defs from registered MCP servers Google ADK with native MCP + Agent2Agent (A2A) protocol Agent Cards for capability discovery; native Qdrant and OpenAPI tool integrations OpenAI Function Calling (JSON Schema) + AgentKit Connector Registry Strict schema enforcement (strict: true); tool count kept under 20 per call for accuracy Salesforce Agentforce + A2A for cross-org agent interop Lifecycle management as first-class concern; governed agent registry

Patterns common to all: - Tool metadata (name, description, JSON Schema, version, owner) is stored separately from tool implementation - Tools are stateless — all context injected as parameters; connection and credentials injected at registration time, never in the LLM context - Tool count per agent call kept under 10–20 — more tools degrade LLM tool selection accuracy - Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) is standard; any breaking schema change = MAJOR bump; model upgrades = MAJOR bump

docs.title: 2.2 The Emerging Open Standard: MCP (Model Context Protocol)
docs.text:
As of early 2026, MCP is the de facto open standard for agent tool registries:

Metric Value Monthly SDK downloads 97M+ (November 2025) Governance Linux Foundation (AAIF) — co-founded by Anthropic, OpenAI, Block Framework support Anthropic Claude, OpenAI AgentKit, Semantic Kernel, Google ADK, LangChain, CrewAI Protocol base JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio (local) or Streamable HTTP (remote) Tool discovery tools/list RPC; .well-known/mcp.json passive discovery Registry entries ~2,000 servers, 407% growth since September 2025 launch

MCP defines tools as stateless callable functions with JSON Schema input contracts — exactly aligned with our architecture's definition of tools as "deterministic connectors or adapters that perform actions or I/O without reasoning."

docs.title: 2.3 Registry Option Evaluation
docs.text:
Three viable free/open-source approaches exist:

Option A: Build custom lightweight registry (FastAPI + Postgres catalog)

A minimal FastAPI service storing tool metadata (name, description, schema, version, endpoint) in Postgres, with a /tools discovery endpoint. Each tool server is a standalone MCP server or Python function.

  • Pros: Full control, minimal dependencies, built in days
  • Cons: Auth (OAuth/Entra), RBAC, audit logging, and multi-server aggregation all require custom builds; does not compose with the MCP ecosystem; ongoing maintenance burden

Option B: LangChain / LangGraph Tool Ecosystem

Tools implemented as LangChain @tool decorators registered into a LangGraph ToolNode. Large ecosystem of pre-built integrations (Postgres, MongoDB, Qdrant, Azure AI Search all have LangChain community tools).

  • Pros: Large pre-built ecosystem; tight LLM integration
  • Cons: Heavy LangChain dependency; not MCP-protocol-compatible; less aligned with our event-driven architecture; proprietary abstraction rather than an open standard

Option C: MCP-native stack with mcp-gateway-registry

All tools exposed as MCP servers (using fastmcp or the mcp Python SDK). A single gateway (agentic-community/mcp-gateway-registry, Apache 2.0) handles auth, RBAC, audit, and multi-server aggregation behind one endpoint.

  • Pros: Industry-standard protocol; universal framework compatibility; built-in auth/RBAC/audit; dynamic tool discovery; free; extensible; vendor-maintained community servers available for most target systems
  • Cons: Gateway adds ~2 days of setup overhead vs a flat list of standalone servers

docs.title: 2.4 Decision
docs.text:
Option C is selected. The MCP-native stack with mcp-gateway-registry from day one. The reasoning:

  • Auth (OAuth / Entra), RBAC, and audit logging are structural requirements that cannot be retrofitted without rewriting every tool server. Building them once at the gateway layer eliminates this risk entirely.
  • We have 5+ target tool servers. A gateway that aggregates them behind a single endpoint is essential for the orchestration layer to remain stable as tools are added.
  • Compliance requirements (EU AI Act high-risk logging, A4I audit trail) require a single enforcement point — the gateway is that point.
  • The ~2 day setup overhead is trivially smaller than the cost of re-implementing auth and audit logging across each server individually.

docs.title: 3. Gateway: mcp-gateway-registry Capability Comparison
docs.text:
Option A: Simple self-hosted MCP servers, no gateway

Capability Available Host individual MCP servers Yes Tool metadata catalog (name, version, schema) Yes (we build it) OAuth / Entra / Keycloak auth No — DIY per server RBAC (which agent can call which tool) No — DIY Audit log (who called what, when, with what args) No — DIY Multiple MCP servers behind one endpoint No — each server has its own address Dynamic tool discovery by autonomous agents No Agent2Agent (A2A) hub No Compliance-ready (EU AI Act high-risk logging) No

Option B: mcp-gateway-registry (Apache 2.0, agentic-community/mcp-gateway-registry)

Capability Available All of the above Yes Multiple MCP servers behind one gateway endpoint Yes (virtual MCP aggregation) OAuth 2.0 (Cognito, Google, GitHub, Entra, Keycloak) Yes, built-in Fine-grained RBAC per tool per agent Yes Full audit log Yes Dynamic tool discovery by agents (natural language) Yes A2A Hub for agent-to-agent communication Yes SKILL.md registry Yes

Setup overhead: The gateway runs a reverse proxy, a registry service, and (optionally) Keycloak. This adds ~2 days of initial setup effort but eliminates the need to implement auth, RBAC, and audit logging independently across each tool server.

(container)   (container)        (container)

docs.title: 4. Reusing Community and Vendor MCP Servers
docs.text: A large portion of the tool surface area is already implemented by vendor-maintained or well-supported community MCP servers. We should reuse these rather than re-implement.

docs.title: 4.1 Inventory of Available MCP Servers
docs.text: Storage System MCP Server Maintainer Status Notes PostgreSQL @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres Anthropic (archived) Reference only Read-only, no pgvector PostgreSQL + pgvector neverinfamous/postgres-mcp Community Active 206 tools, pgvector extension, connection pooling, HTTP+OAuth MongoDB mongodb-js/mongodb-mcp-server MongoDB (official) Public Preview Atlas-required for vector search; stdio default Azure (Blob, AI Search, Service Bus) microsoft/mcp (Azure MCP Server) Microsoft (official) GA 40+ services, 208 tools; Blob read/write, AI Search query, Service Bus (mgmt only) Qdrant qdrant/mcp-server-qdrant Qdrant (official) Stable 2 tools: qdrant-store, qdrant-find; semantic memory layer only LanceDB lancedb/lancedb-mcp-server LanceDB Reference only 3 tools; educational, not production-grade LanceDB (enhanced) applied-ai-systems/aas-lancedb-mcp Community Active 10 tools, BGE-M3 embeddings, dynamic schema evolution Kafka tuannvm/kafka-mcp-server (Go) Community Active produce, consume, list-topics, describe Kafka + RabbitMQ LarsCowe/queue-pilot Community Active 14+ tools, JSON Schema validation for messages, multi-broker RabbitMQ kenliao94/mcp-server-rabbitmq Community Active Basic publish/consume Azure Queue / Service Bus (data-plane) None — Gap Build required (see §8)

docs.title: 4.2 Adoption Strategy
docs.text:
Use directly (minimal wrapping needed): - microsoft/mcp (Azure MCP Server) — already covers Blob, AI Search, Service Bus management; just configure with Managed Identity - mongodb-js/mongodb-mcp-server — official, use for Atlas environments - qdrant/mcp-server-qdrant — official, adequate for semantic memory use case

Use with custom extension (add tools to existing server): - neverinfamous/postgres-mcp — deploy as-is; custom tools for business-specific queries can be added - applied-ai-systems/aas-lancedb-mcp — baseline works; may need tuning for our embedding models

Fork and extend: - LarsCowe/queue-pilot — extend to add Azure Queue Storage data-plane operations (it only covers Kafka/RabbitMQ natively)

Build from scratch (genuine gap): - Azure Queue Storage (message send/receive/peek/ack) — not in microsoft/mcp - Azure Service Bus data-plane (send/receive messages) — microsoft/mcp only exposes management (queue stats, message counts), not message content operations

docs.title: 4.3 Benefit of Reuse
docs.text: By adopting vendor-maintained servers, we automatically receive: - Security patches from MongoDB, Microsoft, Qdrant without our intervention - New tool additions as services evolve (e.g., when Microsoft adds Queue Storage data-plane to Azure MCP Server, we upgrade a container image) - Community-tested tool descriptions and schemas (poor descriptions are the #1 cause of wrong tool selection) - Compliance with each vendor's own auth patterns (Managed Identity for Azure, Atlas service account for MongoDB)

docs.title: 5. Secret Management: Isolating Credentials from the LLM
The Core Guarantee
docs.text: The LLM only sees tool inputs and tool outputs — never the tool's internals. Secrets live in the MCP server process memory and never cross the boundary to the LLM context window.

docs.title: Pattern 1: Environment Variables Bound at Server Startup
docs.text:
When an orchestrator or gateway starts an MCP server (as a subprocess or container), it passes secrets via environment variables. The LLM never sees these values.

Example — PostgreSQL MCP Server:

// mcp-gateway-registry server registration (stored in gateway config, never in LLM context)
{
  "name": "postgres-tools",
  "command": "npx",
  "args": ["-y", "@my-org/postgres-mcp"],
  "env": {
    "POSTGRES_DSN": "postgresql://svc_agent:${SECRET_PG_PASSWORD}@db.internal:5432/a4i_prod",
    "MAX_POOL_SIZE": "10"
  }
}

Inside the MCP server Python process:

import os
import psycopg2
from functools import lru_cache

# Bound once at startup — never passed to LLM as a parameter
DSN = os.environ["POSTGRES_DSN"]

@lru_cache(maxsize=1)
def get_pool():
    return psycopg2.pool.ThreadedConnectionPool(1, 10, DSN)

# The tool schema the LLM sees: only { "sql": string, "params": array }
# The LLM has no way to discover POSTGRES_DSN or request it
def query_tool(sql: str, params: list) -> dict:
    with get_pool().getconn() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(sql, params).fetchall()
    return {"data": rows, "count": len(rows)}

What the LLM sees in the tool call: 

{
  "name": "postgres.query",
  "arguments": {
    "sql": "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE active = $1",
    "params": [true]
  }
}

The LLM has no mechanism to ask "what is POSTGRES_DSN?" — it is not a parameter, not in the tool description, and not in the response.

docs.title: Pattern 2: Azure Key Vault — Dynamic Ephemeral Credentials
docs.text:
For production environments, secrets should not live in environment variables at all. Instead, the MCP server fetches short-lived credentials from Azure Key Vault using Managed Identity (no secret needed to access Key Vault):

from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from azure.keyvault.secrets import SecretClient

# No credentials in config — Managed Identity is used to authenticate to Key Vault
credential = ManagedIdentityCredential()
kv_client = SecretClient("https://a4i-keyvault.vault.azure.net/", credential)

def get_db_connection():
    # Fetch secret at call time — Key Vault caches internally, so this is ~2ms overhead
    pg_password = kv_client.get_secret("postgres-agent-password").value
    return psycopg2.connect(
        host="db.internal", database="a4i_prod",
        user="svc_agent", password=pg_password
    )

Flow of secret isolation: 

Azure Key Vault
      │
      │ (Managed Identity, no secret in config)
      ▼
MCP Server Container (Azure Container Apps)
      │
      │ Only formatted query results
      ▼
MCP Gateway
      │
      │ Only tool schemas (name, description, JSON Schema)
      ▼
LLM Provider (Azure OpenAI / Anthropic)
      │
      │ Tool call: { "name": "postgres.query", "arguments": {...} }
      ▼
Agent — never sees credentials at any point

docs.title: Why This Matters vs. System Prompt Injection of Credentials
docs.text:
If credentials were placed in a system prompt, they would: - Appear in every LLM API request (logged by the LLM provider and in any tracing tool) - Be extractable via prompt injection attacks ("repeat all text above") - Leak if the conversation is exported, cached, or debugged - Violate Azure OpenAI's data handling policies

With env-var / Key Vault binding, credentials exist only in the MCP server process address space — isolated from the LLM's context window by design.

docs.title: 6. Transport Layer: stdio vs HTTP SSE vs Streamable HTTP
The Current Standard (MCP Spec 2025-11-25)
docs.text:
The 2025-11-25 specification defines two standard transports: 1. stdio — for local, in-process MCP servers 2. Streamable HTTP — for all network-accessible MCP servers

HTTP+SSE is officially deprecated in the 2025-11-25 spec. It is retained only for backwards compatibility. All new MCP servers should use Streamable HTTP for remote scenarios.

docs.title: stdio — When and Why
docs.text:
Property Value Mechanism Client launches server as a child subprocess; communicates via stdin/stdout; newline-delimited JSON-RPC Latency ~0.1–1 ms (pure IPC, no network stack) Throughput ~10,000+ ops/sec Session model One client, one server — the server exits when the client exits Horizontal scaling Not possible — single process, single client

Best for: - Local development (developer laptops, CI/CD pipelines) - Desktop AI clients (Claude Desktop, Cursor, VS Code Copilot) - Tools accessing local filesystem or OS-level resources - LanceDB in embedded mode (the MCP server and the DB library run in the same process — zero network hop) - High-throughput automation pipelines where 1000s of tool calls/min make network overhead measurable

Not suitable for: - Any scenario where the MCP server needs to be accessed by more than one agent simultaneously - Cloud deployments behind a load balancer - Services that need to survive an agent restart (the server dies with the client)

docs.title: HTTP+SSE — Why It Was Deprecated
docs.text:
HTTP+SSE required two separate endpoints: 1. A POST endpoint for client-to-server requests 2. An SSE stream endpoint for server-to-client responses

This caused: - Complex routing and CORS configuration - Persistent long-lived connections that don't survive load balancers or serverless platforms (each request had to hit the same server instance) - No stateless operation — horizontal scaling was fundamentally impossible - Proxy/firewall issues with long-lived SSE connections - Connection drops requiring full reconnection and context loss

HTTP+SSE technically still works for backwards compatibility, but building new tools on it is inadvisable.

docs.title: Streamable HTTP — The Correct Choice for Cloud Deployments
docs.text:
Mechanism: Single HTTP endpoint supporting both POST and GET. Client sends JSON-RPC via POST. Server responds with either: - application/json for synchronous responses - text/event-stream (SSE) for streaming/async responses (dynamically chosen per request)

Key improvements over HTTP+SSE:

Feature HTTP+SSE Streamable HTTP Endpoint count 2 (POST + SSE stream) 1 Stateless operation No Yes (optional session via MCP-Session-Id header) Load balancer compatible No Yes Serverless compatible No Yes (Azure Functions, Container Apps scale-to-zero) Resumable streams No Yes (Last-Event-ID header) Security model Weak Origin header validation, protocol version enforcement

For our cloud deployments, Streamable HTTP is the right choice for all MCP servers deployed to Azure Container Apps, AKS, or Azure Functions.

docs.title: Decision Matrix
docs.text: Scenario Transport Developer local tooling, single user stdio LanceDB embedded (in-process DB) stdio Claude Desktop / Cursor integration stdio Azure Container Apps hosted MCP server Streamable HTTP AKS-deployed MCP server, multiple agents Streamable HTTP Azure Functions exposed as MCP tool Streamable HTTP Behind Azure API Management Streamable HTTP Talking to a legacy server (cannot update) HTTP+SSE (backwards compat only)

docs.title: 7. Hosting Options for MCP Servers and the Gateway
Option A: Docker Compose (Development / Small Deployments)
docs.text:
All MCP servers and the gateway run as Docker containers on a single host. Most appropriate for: - Local development environment - Single-VM pilot deployments - Cost-sensitive scenarios (one VM, ~$20-50/month)

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  gateway:
    image: agentic-community/mcp-gateway-registry:latest
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      - AUTH_PROVIDER=keycloak
      - KEYCLOAK_URL=http://keycloak:8080
    depends_on: [keycloak, registry-db]

  postgres-mcp:
    image: my-org/postgres-mcp:1.2.0
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DSN_FILE=/run/secrets/postgres_dsn
    secrets: [postgres_dsn]
    # No port exposure — only accessible to gateway via internal Docker network

  qdrant-mcp:
    image: qdrant/mcp-server-qdrant:latest
    environment:
      - QDRANT_URL=http://qdrant:6333
    depends_on: [qdrant]

  qdrant:
    image: qdrant/qdrant:latest
    volumes: ["qdrant-data:/qdrant/storage"]

  azure-mcp:
    image: mcr.microsoft.com/azure/mcp:latest
    environment:
      - AZURE_CLIENT_ID=${MI_CLIENT_ID}   # Managed Identity
      - AZURE_TENANT_ID=${AZURE_TENANT_ID}

  queue-mcp:
    image: my-org/queue-mcp:1.0.0        # Custom-built (see §8)
    environment:
      - KAFKA_BROKERS=kafka:9092
      - AZURE_SERVICEBUS_CONN_FILE=/run/secrets/sb_conn

  keycloak:
    image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:latest

  registry-db:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    volumes: ["registry-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data"]

secrets:
  postgres_dsn:
    external: true       # Managed outside Docker Compose (e.g., Azure Key Vault, .env)
  sb_conn:
    external: true

Security note: MCP tool servers are not exposed on public ports. Only the gateway is externally accessible. Tool servers communicate with the gateway over the internal Docker network.

docs.title: Option B: Azure Container Apps (Recommended for Cloud)
docs.text:
Azure Container Apps (ACA) is Microsoft's officially recommended hosting for remote MCP servers. It provides: - Scale-to-zero (zero cost when idle) - Managed ingress with TLS - Managed Identity for Azure Key Vault and Azure services (no secrets in config) - Azure Virtual Network integration (tool servers in private subnet)

docs.title: Option C: AKS (Kubernetes) — Production Scale
docs.text:
Two deployment patterns:

Sidecar pattern — MCP server runs in the same pod as the agent, connected via localhost. Zero network latency, suitable for stdio or localhost Streamable HTTP:

# Agent pod with MCP server sidecar
spec:
  containers:
  - name: agent-orchestrator
    image: my-org/orchestrator:latest
    env:
    - name: MCP_POSTGRES_URL
      value: "http://localhost:8001/mcp"  # Sidecar, same pod
  - name: postgres-mcp-sidecar
    image: my-org/postgres-mcp:1.2.0
    ports: [{containerPort: 8001}]
    env:
    - name: POSTGRES_DSN
      valueFrom:
        secretKeyRef: {name: postgres-mcp-secrets, key: dsn}

Dedicated service pattern — MCP servers as independent Kubernetes services; gateway as a shared ingress:

# Gateway deployment with Workload Identity (AKS best practice)
spec:
  serviceAccountName: mcp-gateway-sa  # Bound to Azure Managed Identity via annotation
  containers:
  - name: gateway
    image: agentic-community/mcp-gateway-registry:latest

AKS + Workload Identity is the recommended pattern for production — the pod gets a Managed Identity without any secrets in the deployment manifest.

docs.title: Option D: Azure Functions (Serverless Tool Endpoints)
docs.text:
Individual tools can be exposed as Azure Functions with the MCP binding, rather than as a standalone server. Best for: - Infrequent calls where scale-to-zero matters (cost: ~$0 at rest) - Tools that call other Azure services and want native SDK bindings - Simple tools that don't require a full container

# Azure Function as an MCP tool (Python v2 programming model)
import azure.functions as func

app = func.FunctionApp()

@app.function_name("blob_read")
@app.mcp_tool(name="blob.read", description="Read text content of a blob")
def blob_read_tool(tool_input: dict) -> str:
    from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient
    from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
    client = BlobServiceClient(
        f"https://{STORAGE_ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net",
        credential=ManagedIdentityCredential()
    )
    return client.get_blob_client(
        tool_input["container"], tool_input["name"]
    ).download_blob().readall().decode()

Tradeoff: Cold starts add 200-800ms latency. Not appropriate for tools called many times per agent turn.

docs.title: Latency Reference
docs.text:
Hosting Pattern Transport Typical Overhead Sidecar (same pod, localhost) Streamable HTTP ~1–5 ms ACA internal subnet Streamable HTTP ~2–10 ms AKS ClusterIP service Streamable HTTP ~1–8 ms Cross-region Streamable HTTP ~50–200 ms Azure Functions (warm) Streamable HTTP ~50–150 ms Azure Functions (cold) Streamable HTTP ~300–800 ms

For interactive agent workflows, LLM inference time (1–30s) dominates. MCP transport overhead is negligible in all hosted scenarios except cross-region.

docs.title: 8. Tool Abstractions for Target Storage Systems
Design Principles (Common to All Tools)
docs.text:
1. Stateless: Connections injected at server startup via environment variables or Key Vault — never in tool parameters
  2. Allowlisted operations: Named operations only — no raw query/command passthrough
  3. Structured return envelope: { "data": [...], "count": N, "error": null, "_meta": { "tool": "...", "version": "..." } }
  4. LLM-oriented descriptions: Description field written to guide model tool selection, including when not to use the tool
  5. Namespace prefix: postgres., mongo., blob., qdrant., azure_search., lancedb., queue.

docs.title: 8.1 PostgreSQL Tools (neverinfamous/postgres-mcp extended)
docs.text:
Reuse neverinfamous/postgres-mcp as the base (206 tools, pgvector-aware, connection pooling). Add business-specific query tools as extensions.

Tool Description Key Parameters postgres.query Read-only parameterized SELECT. Never use for writes. sql: str, params: list postgres.upsert Insert or update by conflict key. Returns saved record with ID. table: str, record: dict, conflict_col: str postgres.vector_search Cosine similarity search via pgvector. Returns top-k rows with distance score. table: str, embedding_col: str, query_vector: float[], top_k: int postgres.hybrid_search Combined full-text (tsvector) + pgvector similarity. docs.title: 8.3 Azure Blob Storage Tools (microsoft/mcp + custom extensions)
docs.text:
Use the Microsoft Azure MCP Server (microsoft/mcp) for standard Blob operations. Extend with SAS URL generation for media/document access — this is a gap in the official server that we must fill.

The architecture involves PDFs, images, and binary files. These cannot be returned as raw content in a tool response (size limits, encoding). Instead, agents receive a short-lived signed URL to retrieve or embed the file via a separate HTTP request.

Tool Description Key Parameters blob.list List blob names in a container, filtered by prefix. container: str, prefix: str blob.read Read text content of a blob (UTF-8). Use for text files, JSON, Markdown. Do not use for binary files (PDFs, images) — use blob.download_url instead. container: str, name: str blob.write Write text or JSON content to a blob. Returns blob URL. container: str, name: str, content: str, content_type: str blob.delete Delete a blob. Requires confirm: true to prevent accidental deletion. container: str, name: str, confirm: bool blob.get_metadata Retrieve metadata tags and properties without reading content. container: str, name: str blob.download_url Generate a short-lived SAS URL (default: 15 min) for downloading a blob. Use for PDFs, images, audio, video, or any binary file. container: str, name: str, expiry_minutes: int blob.embedding_url Generate a SAS URL specifically authorized for Azure AI Services to fetch and embed. Returns a URL suitable for passing to an embedding API. Use when the blob is a document or image to be embedded. container: str, name: str

blob.download_url and blob.embedding_url — how they work:

from azure.storage.blob import BlobServiceClient, generate_blob_sas, BlobSasPermissions
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

def download_url(container: str, name: str, expiry_minutes: int = 15) -> dict:
    """
    Generate a SAS URL for downloading a blob. The URL is time-limited.
    The agent never sees the storage account key — it is fetched from Key Vault.
    """
    sas_token = generate_blob_sas(
        account_name=STORAGE_ACCOUNT,
        container_name=container,
        blob_name=name,
        account_key=get_storage_key_from_keyvault(),  # Key Vault, not env var
        permission=BlobSasPermissions(read=True),
        expiry=datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=expiry_minutes)
    )
    return {
        "url": f"https://{STORAGE_ACCOUNT}.blob.core.windows.net/{container}/{name}?{sas_token}",
        "expires_at": (datetime.utcnow() + timedelta(minutes=expiry_minutes)).isoformat(),
        "blob_name": name
    }

The agent receives a URL it can pass to Azure Document Intelligence, Azure OpenAI Vision, or an embedding API — it never has direct storage access. The SAS token is signed server-side and expires automatically.

blob.embedding_url generates a SAS URL with the read permission scoped to a short window (5 minutes default), specifically for passing to embedding/vision APIs. It also enriches the response with content type and blob size metadata to help the agent decide which embedding model to use:

{
  "url": "https://storage.blob.core.windows.net/documents/report.pdf?sv=...&se=...&sig=...",
  "content_type": "application/pdf",
  "size_bytes": 2097152,
  "expires_at": "2026-03-20T14:35:00Z",
  "recommended_model": "azure-document-intelligence"
}

# Azure Queue Storage MCP tool (data-plane — not in microsoft/mcp)
from azure.storage.queue import QueueServiceClient
from azure.identity import ManagedIdentityCredential

credential = ManagedIdentityCredential()
queue_service = QueueServiceClient(
    f"https://{STORAGE_ACCOUNT}.queue.core.windows.net",
    credential=credential
)

def receive_messages(queue: str, max_count: int = 5, lock_duration_secs: int = 30) -> dict:
    """
    Dequeue messages from Azure Queue Storage. Messages are locked (invisible)
    for lock_duration_secs. Call queue.acknowledge with receipt_handle to confirm
    processing. If not acknowledged within the lock duration, message reappears.
    """
    client = queue_service.get_queue_client(queue)
    messages = client.receive_messages(max_messages=max_count, visibility_timeout=lock_duration_secs)
    return {
        "messages": [
            {"id": m.id, "content": m.content, "receipt_handle": m.pop_receipt,
             "dequeue_count": m.dequeue_count}
            for m in messages
        ]
    }

docs.title: 9. VectorStore Abstraction Interface
docs.text:
Tools for Qdrant, LanceDB, and Azure AI Search share a common interface to ensure swap-ability:

from abc import ABC, abstractmethod
from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass
class SearchResult:
    id: str
    text: str
    score: float
    metadata: dict

class VectorStoreAdapter(ABC):
    @abstractmethod
    def search(self, collection: str, query: str, top_k: int = 5,
               filter: dict = None) -> list[SearchResult]: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def upsert(self, collection: str, id: str, text: str,
               metadata: dict = None) -> bool: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def delete(self, collection: str, id: str) -> bool: ...

    @abstractmethod
    def list_collections(self) -> list[str]: ...

# Concrete implementations registered at server startup
class QdrantAdapter(VectorStoreAdapter): ...
class LanceDBAdapter(VectorStoreAdapter): ...        # Embedded, zero network overhead
class AzureAISearchAdapter(VectorStoreAdapter): ...

# MCP tools receive the adapter via DI — same tool schema regardless of backend
class VectorSearchTools:
    def __init__(self, adapter: VectorStoreAdapter):
        self._store = adapter

    @mcp_tool(name="vector.search")
    def search(self, collection: str, query: str, top_k: int = 5) -> list[dict]:
        return [r.__dict__ for r in self._store.search(collection, query, top_k)]

docs.title: Semantic Versioning Rules
docs.text: Change Bump Rationale Rename or remove a required parameter MAJOR Breaks all existing agent configs Change parameter type MAJOR Breaks existing tool calls New optional parameter MINOR Backward-compatible addition Bug fix, no schema change PATCH No agent behavior change Underlying model/embedding upgrade MAJOR Probabilistic output changes even with same schema

docs.text:
Draft → Preview → Stable/GA → Deprecated → Sunset

docs.title: Inclusive Agentic Architecture Template
docs.text: Building Inclusive, Modular, and Agentic Platforms for Education, Healthcare, and Accessibility

docs.title: 1. Abstract
docs.text:
This whitepaper presents an inclusive, agentic architecture designed to enable scalable, modular, and human-centred AI systems across domains such as education, healthcare, and accessibility.

Current digital ecosystems are fragmented, leading to duplication, limited reuse, and difficulty in scaling innovations. The proposed framework unifies these efforts through a layered reference architecture — comprising integration channels, experience orchestration, business logic, agent libraries, and tool adapters under an open and extensible model.

The architecture emphasizes inclusivity, ensuring accessibility via multimodal channels such as mobile, feature phones, and assistive devices. It also embeds security, auditability, and compliance guardrails upfront.

docs.title: 2. Motivation
docs.text:
• Current solutions are point-specific and lack a unified reference model.
  • Fragmentation challenge: Similar patterns solved differently → difficult to reuse, scale, or maintain.
  • Need for a common architectural template that:
  • Reduces duplication of effort across projects.
  • Ensures scalability & reliability during usage surges.
  • Simplifies integration of new datastores and connectors.
  • Embeds security, auditability, and compliance guardrails upfront.

Long-term Vision: A community-driven reference architecture that improves developer onboarding, speeds up experimentation, and ensures enterprise-grade resilience.

docs.title: 3. High-Level Layered Architecture
docs.text: Figure 1: High-Level Agentic Architecture Template

docs.title: 4.1 Integration Layer
docs.text: Serves as the system’s backbone for connectivity and interoperability. It manages authentication, auditing, and compliance across integrations. Main goal: make external data feel internal while maintaining isolation and control.

docs.title: Channels for Access
docs.text: Supports: - Mobile applications - Feature phone–based telecommunications - Web interfaces - Assistive devices (e.g., Hexis, Iris) - Messaging interfaces (WhatsApp, Telegram, SMS)

    User->>ChannelAdapter: Message / Event
    ChannelAdapter->>IntegrationLayer: Normalized request

docs.text: Acts as the central user interaction entry point, normalizing inputs from diverse channels for unified downstream handling. It enriches the data with context, authentication, and personalization cues, and formats output for the appropriate channel.

docs.title: 4.2 Business & Agentic Orchestration Layer
docs.text:
Implements domain-level logic through a hybrid of deterministic services and agentic orchestration.

  • Business Services: Integrate user information, manage persistent data, and handle workflows.
  • Agent-Oriented Orchestration: Delegates reasoning and transformation tasks to agents.

In effect, it acts as the “brain” for domain behaviour, handling branching logic, fallback, error handling, and domain-specific rules or constraints.

docs.title: Agent Library
docs.text:
Agents operate as autonomous reasoning nodes that receive and emit structured events. Each agent processes data and can be chained in different order enabling concurrent reasoning and flexible delegation without direct coupling.

Encapsulates AI reasoning and cognitive tasks into reusable "agents", allowing complex system logic to be broken into small, composable and reusable "units of work".

Agent Type Function Example Use Case RAG Retrieval-Augmented Generation Query knowledge base Translation Multilingual Interaction Local language conversion ASR/TTS Speech Processing IVR / audio channels Consensus Evaluator Group agreement logic Feedback loops Data Sanity Validation and safety Input consistency

Each agent defines input/output contracts and performance expectations for interoperability.

Lifecycle and Agent Invocation

Step 1: Registered in the central Agent Registry under a versioned identifier.

Step 2: Invoked by an Orchestrator or another agent based on workflow logic.

Step 3: Executed with full context (user/session/memory data).

Step 4: Returns standardized output for downstream agents or final rendering.

    participant Orchestrator
    participant AgentRegistry
    participant RAGAgent
    participant TTSAgent

    Orchestrator->>AgentRegistry: Lookup("rag_agent:v1")
    AgentRegistry-->>Orchestrator: Return config & schema
    Orchestrator->>RAGAgent: Execute(query="symptoms of dengue")
    RAGAgent-->>Orchestrator: Return summary + confidence
    Orchestrator->>TTSAgent: Convert text → speech
    TTSAgent-->>Orchestrator: Return audio file reference

docs.text:
Tools are deterministic connectors or adapters that perform actions or I/O without reasoning.

Tool Purpose Example WhatsApp Adapter Messaging Send notifications IVR Gateway Telephony Play prompts Email Tool Communication Send updates CRM Adapter External Systems Update lead data MongoDB Adapter Storage Persist structured data

Real World Example: Sahayak Orchestrator

The Sahayak Orchestrator exemplifies how these architectural layers operate in unison. - It receives user inputs—along with historical context and session memory—and determines which agents or tools should act next. - Using its centralized Tool Registry, populated with system-level MCP (Multi-Channel Plugin) abstractions, the orchestrator dynamically routes requests to the appropriate agents for reasoning and to the corresponding tools for deterministic execution. - This event-driven workflow enables Sahayak to coordinate human-like reasoning with system-level precision, ensuring adaptive, multimodal interactions across channels and services.

    Orchestrator->>Agent: SahayakTextRequestEvent
    Agent->>Tool: ToolCallRequestEvent (resolved via known_tool_owners)
    Tool->>ExternalService: Executes operation (e.g., send message)
    ExternalService-->>Tool: Returns API result
    Tool-->>Agent: ToolCallExecutionEvent (structured response)
    Agent-->>Orchestrator: Final message event
    Orchestrator-->>ExperienceLayer: Rendered response

docs.title: 4.3 Ingestion Layer
docs.text: converts raw or semi-structured content (textbooks, media, logs) into enriched, searchable knowledge representations for downstream agents. Supports high-throughput ingestion, context caching, and long-term knowledge storage.

docs.title: 7. Limitations & Future Considerations
docs.text:
• Complex Orchestration: Debugging multi-agent workflows may be non-trivial.
  • Connectivity Dependency: Cloud-dependent features (RAG, ASR/TTS) may face offline limitations.

  • Maintenance Overhead: Hybrid agentic-service systems require continuous synchronization and version management.

docs.title: Purpose and Scope
docs.text:
This document proposes a common, cross-cutting governance and safety framework that embeds compliance, cost control, and safety into every AI interaction across digital public AI goods:

  • BYOEB (ASHA WhatsApp RAG for healthcare) — healthcare compliance
  • Shiksha Copilot (lesson outcome–driven education copilot) — education compliance
  • SEEDS (audio-first IVR and conferencing for visually impaired learners) — education + accessibility compliance

…and is extensible to new products, domains, and regulatory requirements.

It aligns with the Inclusive Architecture as a horizontal layer that wraps around the Business & Agentic Orchestration Layer — "request guard → consent check → cost tracking → LLM call → response guard → audit logging" — and implements those as reusable agents and tools across domains.

📖 Related: The LLM call step is abstracted through the LLM Gateway Layer, which provides unified access to multiple LLM providers with built-in cost tracking, failover, and guardrails.

docs.title: Design Drivers
docs.text:
1. Aligned with Inclusive Architecture

    • Governance is a cross-cutting concern serving multiple domains (healthcare, education, accessibility) via common agents & tools.
    • All products interact with AI through governance-wrapped interfaces; governance itself is multi-tenant and domain-aware.

  2. Multi-Regulation

    • Healthcare: PHI protection, clinical data handling
    • Education: Student data protection, minor data handling
    • General: Data privacy, security controls
    • AI-Specific: Transparency, accountability, bias prevention

  3. Multi-Concern

    • Consent & Privacy: Verifiable consent management (parental consent, data processing authorization)
    • Data Protection: PII/PHI detection, anonymization, retention policies
    • Cost Control: Token tracking, budget enforcement, usage optimization
    • Safety: Content moderation, hallucination detection, topic guards
    • Audit: Comprehensive logging, compliance reporting, breach detection

  4. Domain-Aware but Reusable

    • BYOEB's healthcare compliance (PHI handling) should be a profile on top of generic governance steps.
    • Shiksha's education compliance (parental consent, student data) should be the default education profile.
    • SEEDS' accessibility considerations should extend the education profile.

  5. Non-Blocking & Observable

    • Governance adds minimal latency to AI interactions.
    • Strong observability for compliance audits and incident response.
    • Human-in-the-loop escalation for edge cases.

docs.title: Conceptual Model
docs.text:
We define three layers inside the governance system (itself mapped as a horizontal wrapper in the Inclusive Architecture):

  1. Guard Layer: Request and response interception with policy evaluation.
  2. Engine Layer: Consent, Cost, Safety, and Audit engines that implement governance logic.
  3. Policy & Configuration Layer: Domain profiles, regulatory mappings, and tenant configuration.

docs.title: High-Level Governance Flow
docs.text:
The governance flow maps to the Inclusive Architecture layers while progressively enriching the GovernanceContext—a data structure that flows with each request.

Step Description IA Layer Governance Concept Context Field Enriched 1. Request Received User request arrives via channel Integration — request_id, channel 2. Context Initialization Create GovernanceContext, resolve user/tenant Experience GovernanceContext user_id, tenant_id, domain_profile 3. Consent Resolution Query for user's consent status Experience Engine Layer: Consent consent_status 4. Budget Resolution Query Gateway for spend status Experience LLM Gateway budget_status 5. Request Guards Evaluate consent guards, budget alerts Business & Agentic Guard Layer: Request guard_results 6. Domain PII Handling Detect domain-specific PII (PHI, education) & anonymize Business & Agentic Engine Layer: Safety anonymization_mapping_id 7. LLM Execution Call LLM via Gateway (generic PII + moderation) Business & Agentic LLM Gateway gateway_request_id 8. Response Guards Evaluate output compliance, deanonymize domain PII Business & Agentic Guard Layer: Response response_guard_results 9. Cost Capture Extract cost/tokens from Gateway response Business & Agentic LLM Gateway cost, tokens_used, model_used 10. Audit Logging Log governance-specific events (guards, consent) Business & Agentic Engine Layer: Audit — (persisted) 11. Response Delivery Return response to user via channel Integration — —

📖 Gateway vs Governance Responsibilities: See What the Gateway Provides vs What Governance Adds below for detailed responsibility boundaries.

We implement each step as one or more agents (reasoning/policy-heavy) and tools (IO or deterministic work).

docs.title: GovernanceContext: The Canonical Data Model
docs.text:
The GovernanceContext is an in-memory data structure that flows through Inclusive Architecture layers, getting enriched at each step. It is NOT a separate application—rather, it's the "request context" for governance operations.

Field Description LiteLLM Mapping Storage request_id UUID for this governance request metadata.request_id governance_audit_events correlation_id UUID linking related requests metadata.correlation_id governance_audit_events tenant_id Tenant/partner/org context metadata.team_id (virtual key) governance_audit_events user_id User making the request metadata.user_id (spend tracking) governance_audit_events domain_profile health_byoeb / education_shiksha / etc. metadata.domain_profile governance_audit_events consent_status Map of consent types to status — consent_records budget_status Current spend vs. limits (queried from Gateway) — — (read from LiteLLM_TeamTable) anonymization_mapping_id Reference to domain PII mapping for deanonymization metadata.anon_mapping_id anonymization_mappings gateway_request_id LiteLLM's request ID for correlation Response id — (stored in LiteLLM_SpendLogs) cost Request cost in USD Response response_cost — (stored in LiteLLM_SpendLogs) tokens_used Total tokens consumed Response usage.total_tokens — (stored in LiteLLM_SpendLogs) model_used Actual model that served the request Response model — (stored in LiteLLM_SpendLogs) guard_results Results from request/response guards — governance_audit_events audit_metadata Timestamps, IP, user agent, regulations — governance_audit_events

📝 Storage Principle: Fields with LiteLLM mapping are stored by the Gateway—governance queries them, doesn't duplicate. Governance only stores compliance-specific data (consent, guard decisions, anonymization mappings).

docs.title: How the System Works
docs.text:
1. GovernanceContext flows through Inclusive Architecture layers:

flowchart LR
    subgraph Request Flow
        A[User Request] --> B[Integration Layer]
        B --> C[Experience Layer]
        C --> D[Business & Agentic Layer]
    end
    subgraph Governance Engine
        B --> B1[context created]
        B1 --"request_id, channel" --> B
        C --> C1[context enriched]
        C1 --"user_id, tenant_id, consent_status, budget_status" --> C
    end
    subgraph LLM Gateway 
        D1[+guards + audit] --> E   
        D --> D1
        E[LLM Invocation] --> D1
    end

2. Governance Engines are stateful services the context interacts with:

flowchart TB
    subgraph Governance Tools
        CE[ConsentEngine<br/>getStatus, request, verify]
        COE[CostEngine<br/>getBudget, alert]
        SE[SafetyEngine<br/>anonymize, deanonymize]
        AE[AuditEngine<br/>log, query, export]
    end

    subgraph Storage
        PG[(PostgreSQL<br/>Governance Schema)]
    end

    CE --> PG
    COE --> PG
    SE --> PG
    AE --> PG

3. LLM Gateway receives context as metadata:

sequenceDiagram
    participant GC as GovernanceContext
    participant GW as LLM Gateway (LiteLLM)
    participant LLM as LLM Provider

    GC->>GW: completion(model, messages, metadata)
    Note right of GC: metadata = {<br/>request_id,<br/>team_id (tenant),<br/>user_id,<br/>domain_profile<br/>}

Summary: GovernanceContext is a data structure that flows with the request through Inclusive Architecture layers. It interacts with Governance Engines (stateful services) to resolve consent, budget, and safety status, and passes relevant fields to the LLM Gateway as metadata. After the LLM call, cost and usage data from the Gateway enriches the context before final audit logging.

docs.title: Core Implementation
docs.text: ⚠️ Implementation Layering: This framework builds ON TOP of the LLM Gateway Layer. The gateway provides foundational capabilities (unified LLM API, cost tracking, generic PII detection, content moderation, rate limiting, observability). This governance framework adds domain-specific compliance logic that the gateway cannot provide: consent management, regulatory audit trails, PHI/education-specific guards, and compliance reporting.

docs.title: What the Gateway Provides vs What Governance Adds
docs.text: Capability LLM Gateway (LiteLLM) Governance Framework LLM routing & failover ✅ Built-in — Cost calculation ✅ Per-request automatic Compliance cost reports Budget enforcement ✅ Per-key/team blocking Alert thresholds, compliance attribution Generic PII detection ✅ Presidio integration — Domain PII (PHI, education) ❌ ✅ Domain-specific guards Content moderation ✅ OpenAI/LlamaGuard — Prompt injection ✅ Lakera integration — Topic restrictions ❌ Generic only ✅ Domain-specific topic lists Age-appropriate content ❌ ✅ Minor data protection guards Consent management ❌ ✅ Domain-specific consent LLM call logging ✅ Full metadata — Governance events ❌ ✅ Consent, guard decisions Compliance reports ❌ ✅ Regulatory exports Retention policies ❌ ✅ Configurable per domain

docs.title: Guard Layer
docs.text:
Request Guard:

Guards intercept requests before they reach the agentic layer. A guard evaluates a request and returns one of: - ALLOW — Request proceeds unchanged - BLOCK — Request is rejected with reason - MODIFY — Request content is transformed (e.g., PII anonymized) - ESCALATE — Request requires human review

interface RequestGuard {
  evaluate(request: GovernanceRequest): Promise<GuardResult>;
}

interface GuardResult {
  decision: 'allow' | 'block' | 'modify' | 'escalate';
  reason?: string;
  modifiedContent?: string;
  violations?: string[];
}

Guard Types:

  1. Consent Guards (Governance-specific — not in gateway)

    • ParentalConsentGuard — Verify parental consent for minors
    • DataProcessingAuthorizationGuard — Verify data processing authorization
    • DisclosureConsentGuard — Verify data disclosure consent

  2. Safety Guards (Mixed — some leverage gateway, some governance-specific)

    • PIIDetectionGuard — Delegates to gateway's Presidio integration
    • PHIFilterGuard — Governance-specific: healthcare PHI beyond generic PII
    • ContentModerationGuard — Delegates to gateway's OpenAI/LlamaGuard integration
    • TopicRestrictionGuard — Governance-specific: domain-aware topic filtering
    • MinorDataGuard — Governance-specific: age-appropriate content for minors

  3. Cost Guards (Leverage gateway with governance extensions)

    • BudgetGuard — Queries gateway's spend tracking + governance alert thresholds
    • RateLimitGuard — Delegates to gateway's per-key rate limiting

Response Guard:

Guards validate AI-generated responses before returning to users.

  1. Compliance Guards (Governance-specific — not in gateway)

    • PHIDisclosureGuard — Prevent unauthorized PHI in responses
    • MinorDataGuard — Extra protection for children's data

  2. Quality Guards (Governance-specific — domain-aware validation)

    • HallucinationDetectionGuard — Flag potential fabricated content
    • SourceAttributionGuard — Ensure RAG responses cite sources

  3. Restoration Guards (Governance-specific — reversible anonymization)

    • DeAnonymizationGuard — Restore original values using stored mapping

docs.title: Engine Layer
docs.text:
1. Consent Engine

Manages user consent across regulatory requirements.

interface ConsentEngine {
  checkConsent(userId, consentType, dataCategory): Promise<boolean>;
  requestConsent(userId, consentType, scope): Promise<ConsentRequest>;
  verifyConsent(consentId, verificationData): Promise<boolean>;
  withdrawConsent(userId, consentType): Promise<void>;
  getConsentHistory(userId): Promise<ConsentRecord[]>;
}

Consent Types:

  • PARENTAL_CONSENT — Verifiable parental consent for minors
  • DISCLOSURE_CONSENT — Authorization for data disclosure
  • DATA_PROCESSING_AUTHORIZATION — Sensitive data processing authorization
  • AI_PROCESSING — General AI processing consent
  • DATA_RETENTION — Consent for data storage beyond session

Parental Consent Verification Methods:

  • Credit card micro-transaction
  • Knowledge-based authentication
  • Government ID verification
  • Video call verification

2. Cost Engine

Extends the LLM Gateway Layer's built-in cost tracking with governance-specific capabilities.

📖 Gateway Provides: Per-request cost calculation, virtual key budgets, spend tracking database, per-team/per-key limits. See LLM Gateway Layer Cost Tracking for implementation details and code examples.

Governance Framework Adds:

interface GovernanceCostEngine {
  // ── PROACTIVE (before LLM call) ──
  // Query gateway for current spend, trigger warning alerts
  checkBudgetStatus(tenantId): Promise<BudgetStatus>;
  checkAlertThreshold(tenantId): Promise<AlertStatus>;

  // ── REACTIVE (after LLM call / on-demand) ──
  // Query gateway data for compliance reporting (no duplication)
  queryGatewaySpend(tenantId, dateRange): Promise<SpendData>;
  getUsageSummary(tenantId, domainProfile?, dateRange): Promise<UsageSummary>;
  generateCostReport(tenantId, regulation, dateRange): Promise<CostReport>;

  // ── CONFIGURATION ──
  configureAlerts(tenantId, alertConfig): Promise<void>;
  getAlertHistory(tenantId): Promise<AlertEvent[]>;
}

🔑 Key Principle: Cost Engine QUERIES the Gateway—it does NOT duplicate storage. All cost/usage data lives in LiteLLM_SpendLogs.

Proactive vs Reactive Behavior:

Behavior When What Happens Proactive Before LLM call Query Gateway spend → check against governance_alert_config → send warning if >80% Reactive After LLM call Gateway records cost automatically; governance queries for reports

Governance-Specific Extensions:

Capability Gateway (LiteLLM) Governance Framework Adds Cost calculation ✅ Per-request automatic — (use gateway) Budget enforcement ✅ Per-key/team blocking Proactive: Alert thresholds before blocking (80% warning) Spend tracking ✅ PostgreSQL tables — (query gateway, don't duplicate) Reporting Basic spend queries Reactive: Compliance-formatted reports per domain Attribution Team/key level Reactive: User + domain profile + regulation context in reports

3. Safety Engine

Extends the LLM Gateway Layer's built-in guardrails with domain-specific safety logic.

📖 Gateway Provides: Generic PII detection (Presidio), prompt injection protection (Lakera), content moderation (OpenAI Moderation, LlamaGuard), custom guardrail hooks. See LLM Gateway Layer Guardrails for implementation details and configuration examples.

Governance Framework Adds:

interface GovernanceSafetyEngine {
  // ── PROACTIVE (before LLM call) ──
  // Domain-specific PII beyond gateway's generic detection
  detectDomainPII(text, domainProfile): Promise<DomainPIIDetection[]>;
  // Reversible anonymization (gateway's Presidio is one-way)
  anonymizeWithMapping(text, detections): Promise<{text: string, mapping: AnonymizationMapping}>;
  // Domain-specific topic compliance
  checkTopicCompliance(text, domainProfile): Promise<TopicResult>;
  // Age-appropriate content filtering
  checkAgeAppropriateness(text, userAge): Promise<AgeComplianceResult>;

  // ── REACTIVE (after LLM call) ──
  // Restore original values in response using stored mapping
  deanonymize(text, mappingId): string;
  // Check response for PHI disclosure
  checkResponseCompliance(response, domainProfile): Promise<ComplianceResult>;
}

🔑 Key Principle: Safety Engine adds domain-specific detection (PHI, education records) ON TOP of Gateway's generic PII. It also provides reversible anonymization with mapping storage.

Proactive vs Reactive Behavior:

Behavior When What Happens Proactive Before LLM call Detect domain PII → anonymize with mapping → store mapping → send to Gateway Reactive After LLM call Retrieve mapping → deanonymize response → check for unauthorized disclosure

Governance-Specific Extensions:

Capability Gateway (LiteLLM) Governance Framework Adds Generic PII (name, email, phone) ✅ Presidio integration — (use gateway) PHI detection (healthcare identifiers) ❌ Not domain-aware Proactive: PHIFilterGuard with MRN, conditions, medications Education PII (student ID, grades) ❌ Not domain-aware Proactive: EducationDataGuard with education-specific entities Content moderation ✅ OpenAI/LlamaGuard — (use gateway) Prompt injection ✅ Lakera integration — (use gateway) Topic restrictions ❌ Generic only Proactive: Domain-specific topic lists per profile Age-appropriate content ❌ Not available Proactive: MinorDataGuard for minor data protection Reversible anonymization ❌ One-way only Proactive + Reactive: Mapping storage → deanonymization Response compliance ❌ Not available Reactive: PHI disclosure check, minor data protection

4. Audit Engine

Extends the LLM Gateway Layer's logging with compliance-specific audit trails.

📖 Gateway Provides: Request/response metadata, token counts, costs, latency, model used, error details, callbacks to observability platforms (Langfuse, Prometheus, OpenTelemetry). See LLM Gateway Layer Audit Logging for implementation details and observability setup.

Governance Framework Adds:

interface GovernanceAuditEngine {
  // ── REACTIVE (during/after request processing) ──
  // Log governance-specific events (not LLM call metadata)
  logConsentEvent(event: ConsentEvent): Promise<string>;
  logGuardDecision(context: GovernanceContext, result: GuardResult): Promise<string>;
  logPIIEvent(event: PIIEvent): Promise<string>;

  // Link governance audit to gateway logs (via gateway_request_id)
  linkToGatewayLog(governanceEventId, gatewayRequestId): Promise<void>;

  // ── ON-DEMAND (compliance reporting) ──
  // Query governance events + gateway logs for unified reports
  generateComplianceReport(tenantId, regulation, dateRange): Promise<ComplianceReport>;
  exportForRegulator(tenantId, regulation, dateRange): Promise<RegulatoryExport>;

  // ── SCHEDULED (background jobs) ──
  // Retention policy enforcement per regulation
  enforceRetention(regulation): Promise<RetentionResult>;
  // Breach detection patterns
  detectAnomalies(tenantId, dateRange): Promise<AnomalyReport>;
}

🔑 Key Principle: Audit Engine logs governance-specific events (consent, guards, PII handling) to governance_audit_events. It links to Gateway logs via gateway_request_id for unified compliance reporting—it does NOT duplicate LLM call data.

Proactive vs Reactive Behavior:

Behavior When What Happens Reactive During request Log consent checks, guard decisions, PII detection events Reactive After request Link governance event to Gateway log via gateway_request_id On-Demand Compliance audit Query governance events + Gateway logs → generate unified report Scheduled Background Enforce retention policies, detect anomalies/breaches

Governance-Specific Extensions:

Capability Gateway (LiteLLM) Governance Framework Adds LLM call logging ✅ Full request/response — (use gateway) Token/cost tracking ✅ Per-request automatic — (use gateway) Latency metrics ✅ Built-in — (use gateway) Observability export ✅ Langfuse, Prometheus — (use gateway) Consent events ❌ Not tracked Reactive: CONSENT_CHECKED, CONSENT_GRANTED, CONSENT_WITHDRAWN Guard decisions ❌ Not tracked Reactive: REQUEST_BLOCKED, REQUEST_MODIFIED, ESCALATION_TRIGGERED PII detection events ❌ Not tracked Reactive: PII_DETECTED, PII_ANONYMIZED, PII_DEANONYMIZED Compliance reports ❌ Generic queries only On-Demand: Domain-specific audit reports, disclosure logs Regulatory retention ❌ Not enforced Scheduled: Configurable retention per domain profile Breach detection ❌ Not available Scheduled: Unusual access patterns, unauthorized disclosure alerts

docs.title: Governance Pipeline Orchestration
docs.text:
Static Orchestration with Policy-Driven Guards:

The governance framework uses declarative, static pipelines — NOT LLM-driven decision-making for governance. This is deliberate:

Aspect Our Approach Alternative (LLM Governance) Guard sequencing Defined in config, runs deterministically LLM decides which guards to apply LLM usage Only within safety engines (e.g., content moderation) Also for policy decisions Predictability High — same request gets same governance Variable — LLM may interpret policies differently Auditability Full — policy version = exact behavior Partial — depends on LLM reasoning Compliance Provable — regulators can verify logic Uncertain — LLM decisions are opaque

Why static orchestration?

  • Governance requires predictability — the same request must be treated the same way.
  • Compliance audits require provable behavior — we must show exactly what logic was applied.
  • Guards are already policy-rich — they encode regulatory requirements, not general reasoning.
  • Cost-efficient: No reasoning overhead for clear-cut compliance decisions.

Example pipeline configuration:

governance_pipeline: byoeb_healthcare_v1
domain_profile: health_byoeb
request_guards:
  - guard: DataProcessingAuthorizationGuard
    config: { authorization_types: ["treatment", "payment", "operations"] }
  - guard: PHIFilterGuard
    config: { anonymize: true, hash_algorithm: "sha256" }
  - guard: BudgetGuard
    config: { check_user: true, check_tenant: true }
  - guard: ContentModerationGuard
response_guards:
  - guard: PHIDisclosureGuard
  - guard: DeAnonymizationGuard
  - guard: HallucinationDetectionGuard
    config: { threshold: 0.7 }
engines:
  consent:
    store: postgres
    verification_methods: ["knowledge_based"]
  cost:
    pricing_version: "2024-12"
    daily_budget: 100
    monthly_budget: 2000
  audit:
    retention_days: 365
    export_format: json

docs.title: Storage & Registration Layer
docs.text:
📖 Storage Split: Usage/cost data lives in the LLM Gateway's database. Governance maintains separate stores for compliance-specific data.

Governance-Specific Stores (not in gateway):

1. Consent Store

interface ConsentStore {
  save(consent: ConsentRecord): Promise<void>;
  getActiveConsent(userId, consentType): Promise<ConsentRecord | null>;
  getConsentHistory(userId): Promise<ConsentRecord[]>;
  update(consent: ConsentRecord): Promise<void>;
}
  • Implementation: PostgreSQL consent_records table with encryption at rest
  • Retention: Per domain profile configuration (e.g., healthcare: 6 years, education: 5 years)

2. Governance Audit Store (not LLM call logs)

interface GovernanceAuditStore {
  logGovernanceEvent(event: GovernanceAuditEvent): Promise<void>;
  getConsentEvents(tenantId, userId?, dateRange): Promise<ConsentEvent[]>;
  getGuardDecisions(tenantId, dateRange): Promise<GuardDecision[]>;
  exportComplianceReport(tenantId, regulation, dateRange): Promise<ExportResult>;
}
  • Implementation: PostgreSQL governance_audit_events table
  • Retention: Per domain profile configuration
  • Note: LLM request/response logs are in the gateway's LiteLLM_SpendLogs

3. Anonymization Mapping Store

interface AnonymizationStore {
  saveMapping(requestId, mapping): Promise<string>;
  getMapping(mappingId): Promise<AnonymizationMapping | null>;
  expireMapping(mappingId): Promise<void>;
}
  • Implementation: PostgreSQL anonymization_mappings table
  • Short-lived: Mappings expire after response delivery

4. Policy Store

interface PolicyStore {
  getDomainProfile(profileName): Promise<DomainProfile>;
  getGovernancePipeline(pipelineName): Promise<GovernancePipeline>;
  getTenantConfig(tenantId): Promise<TenantConfig>;
}
  • Implementation: YAML files in git (versioned) + runtime cache
  • Tenant overrides stored in PostgreSQL

Gateway Data Access (query, don't duplicate):

interface GatewayDataAccess {
  // Query LiteLLM's spend tracking
  getTenantSpend(tenantId, dateRange): Promise<SpendSummary>;
  getUserSpend(userId, tenantId, dateRange): Promise<SpendSummary>;

  // Query LiteLLM's request logs for compliance reports
  getRequestLogs(tenantId, dateRange, filters?): Promise<RequestLog[]>;
}
  • Implementation: Read-only queries against LiteLLM's PostgreSQL tables
  • Used for: Compliance cost reports, usage attribution

docs.title: Multi-Tenant Support
docs.text:
Every governance operation is scoped to a tenant:

  • tenant.slug determines storage partitions (consent, usage, audit tables)
  • Tenant-specific budget limits and policy overrides
  • Tenant-specific consent configurations

Tenant–Profile Relationship:

A single tenant can operate across multiple domain profiles. For example, a healthcare education company might use: - health_byoeb profile for patient-facing content - education_shiksha profile for provider training content

The governance context carries both tenant_id and domain_profile, allowing: - Shared billing and usage tracking across profiles - Profile-specific consent and compliance requirements - Unified audit trail across all interactions

docs.title: How This Hooks Back into the Agentic Layer
docs.text:
📖 Gateway Internals: For detailed Gateway architecture and internals, see LLM Gateway Layer Architecture.

From the Agent Orchestrator's point of view, Governance is a wrapper that layers on top of the LLM Gateway.

Governance-Specific Tools (not provided by gateway):

  • Tool: check_consent

    • Inputs: { user_id, consent_type, data_category }
    • Output: { has_consent, reason }
    • Why governance-specific: Domain-specific consent tracking (parental, data processing authorization)

  • Tool: check_domain_compliance

    • Inputs: { text, domain_profile }
    • Output: { compliant, violations[] }
    • Why governance-specific: Domain-aware rules (PHI handling, age-appropriate content)

  • Tool: anonymize_with_mapping

    • Inputs: { text, domain_profile }
    • Output: { anonymized_text, mapping }
    • Why governance-specific: Reversible anonymization for response restoration

  • Tool: log_governance_event

    • Inputs: { event_type, context, details }
    • Output: { event_id }
    • Why governance-specific: Compliance audit trail (consent events, guard decisions)

This gives one Governance interface for all three systems & any new ones, while leveraging the LLM Gateway Layer for foundational LLM operations.

docs.title: Database Architecture
docs.text: ⚠️ Gateway vs Governance Storage: The LLM Gateway Layer (LiteLLM) maintains its own PostgreSQL database for spend tracking, usage records, and request logging. The governance framework maintains separate tables for compliance-specific data that the gateway doesn't track.

docs.title: What the Gateway Already Stores
docs.text:
📖 Gateway Logging Details: For what data the Gateway logs and how to configure observability, see LLM Gateway Layer Audit Logging.

The LLM Gateway (LiteLLM) provides these tables out-of-the-box — do not duplicate:

LiteLLM Table Purpose Governance Access LiteLLM_SpendLogs Per-request cost, tokens, model, latency Query for compliance reports LiteLLM_UserTable User spend totals, budgets Query for budget status LiteLLM_TeamTable Team/tenant spend, limits Map to governance tenants LiteLLM_VerificationToken Virtual keys with budgets Manage via LiteLLM API

Integration Pattern: Query LiteLLM's database for cost/usage data; don't maintain separate usage tables.

docs.title: Governance-Specific Tables
docs.text:
These tables store data the gateway cannot provide:

tenants (shared with Ingestion Framework) 

CREATE TABLE tenants (
  id            UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  slug          TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL,
  display_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  litellm_team_id TEXT,                       -- Maps to LiteLLM team for spend queries
  created_at    TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

consent_records — regulatory consent tracking (not in gateway) 

CREATE TABLE consent_records (
  id                  UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id           UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  user_id             TEXT NOT NULL,
  consent_type        TEXT NOT NULL,           -- 'PARENTAL_CONSENT', 'DATA_PROCESSING_AUTHORIZATION', 'DISCLOSURE_CONSENT'
  status              TEXT NOT NULL,           -- 'pending', 'granted', 'denied', 'withdrawn', 'expired'
  data_categories     JSONB NOT NULL,          -- ['ai_processing', 'phi_access']
  processing_purposes JSONB NOT NULL,
  third_parties       JSONB,
  requested_at        TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  granted_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  expires_at          TIMESTAMPTZ,
  withdrawn_at        TIMESTAMPTZ,
  verification_method TEXT,                    -- 'credit_card', 'knowledge_based', 'video_call'
  verified_by         TEXT,                    -- parent/guardian user ID for parental consent
  ip_address          INET,
  user_agent          TEXT,
  UNIQUE(tenant_id, user_id, consent_type)
);

CREATE INDEX idx_consent_user ON consent_records(tenant_id, user_id, status);

governance_audit_events — compliance-specific events (not LLM call logs) 

-- NOTE: LLM request/response logging is in LiteLLM's SpendLogs table.
-- This table is ONLY for governance-specific events the gateway doesn't track.

CREATE TABLE governance_audit_events (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  timestamp       TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  event_type      TEXT NOT NULL,              -- Governance events only (see below)
  request_id      UUID,                       -- Links to LiteLLM SpendLogs if applicable
  user_id         TEXT,

  -- Consent events
  consent_type    TEXT,
  consent_status  TEXT,

  -- Guard decision events  
  guard_name      TEXT,
  guard_decision  TEXT,                       -- 'allow', 'block', 'modify', 'escalate'
  guard_reason    TEXT,
  violations      JSONB,

  -- PII/PHI events (domain-specific detection)
  pii_types_detected JSONB,                   -- ['mrn', 'health_condition', 'student_id']
  anonymization_mapping_id UUID,              -- Reference to stored mapping for deanonymization

  -- Metadata
  domain_profile  TEXT,
  ip_address      INET,
  user_agent      TEXT,
  metadata        JSONB
);

CREATE INDEX idx_gov_audit_tenant_date ON governance_audit_events(tenant_id, timestamp);
CREATE INDEX idx_gov_audit_request ON governance_audit_events(request_id);
CREATE INDEX idx_gov_audit_type ON governance_audit_events(tenant_id, event_type, timestamp);

Governance Event Types (what this table tracks): - CONSENT_REQUESTED, CONSENT_GRANTED, CONSENT_DENIED, CONSENT_WITHDRAWN - GUARD_BLOCK, GUARD_MODIFY, GUARD_ESCALATE - DOMAIN_PII_DETECTED (PHI, education records — beyond gateway's generic PII) - ANONYMIZATION_APPLIED, DEANONYMIZATION_APPLIED - COMPLIANCE_VIOLATION, ESCALATION_CREATED

anonymization_mappings — reversible anonymization storage (not in gateway) 

CREATE TABLE anonymization_mappings (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  tenant_id       UUID REFERENCES tenants(id),
  request_id      UUID NOT NULL,
  mapping         JSONB NOT NULL,             -- {'[REDACTED_MRN_1]': 'MRN123456', ...}
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  expires_at      TIMESTAMPTZ,                -- Auto-cleanup after response delivered
  used_at         TIMESTAMPTZ                 -- When deanonymization was applied
);

CREATE INDEX idx_anon_request ON anonymization_mappings(request_id);

governance_pipelines — versioned governance configurations (not in gateway) 

CREATE TABLE governance_pipelines (
  id              UUID PRIMARY KEY,
  name            TEXT NOT NULL,              -- 'byoeb_health_v1'
  domain_profile  TEXT NOT NULL,
  version         TEXT NOT NULL,
  config_yaml     TEXT NOT NULL,              -- Full pipeline config
  is_default      BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false,
  created_at      TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE(name, version)
);

governance_alert_config — alert thresholds beyond gateway's hard limits (governance extension) 

-- NOTE: Budget enforcement (blocking) is in LiteLLM via virtual key limits.
-- This table configures warning alerts BEFORE the gateway blocks.

CREATE TABLE governance_alert_config (
  tenant_id                 UUID REFERENCES tenants(id) PRIMARY KEY,
  daily_warning_threshold   INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 80,   -- % of LiteLLM budget
  monthly_warning_threshold INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 80,
  alert_channels            JSONB,                         -- ['email', 'slack', 'webhook']
  alert_recipients          JSONB,
  updated_at                TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

docs.title: Guard & Engine Abstractions
docs.text:
Guard Interface

All guards implement a common protocol:

class Guard(Protocol):
    name: str

    async def evaluate(self, context: GovernanceContext) -> GuardResult:
        ...

Where: 

@dataclass
class GuardResult:
    decision: GuardDecision  # ALLOW, BLOCK, MODIFY, ESCALATE
    reason: str | None = None
    modified_content: str | None = None
    violations: list[str] | None = None
    metadata: dict | None = None

Engine Interfaces

🔑 Design Principle: Engines are categorized by their relationship to the Gateway: - Governance-Only: No Gateway equivalent (Consent) - Gateway-Extending: Adds domain-specific logic on top of Gateway (Safety) - Gateway-Querying: Queries Gateway data, adds governance alerting/reporting (Cost, Audit)

1. Consent Engine (Governance-Only — no Gateway equivalent)

class ConsentEngine(Protocol):
    """Regulatory consent tracking. Fully governance-specific."""
    # PROACTIVE: Check before processing
    async def check(self, user_id: str, consent_type: str, category: str) -> bool: ...

    # REACTIVE: Manage consent lifecycle
    async def request(self, user_id: str, consent_type: str, scope: dict) -> str: ...
    async def verify(self, consent_id: str, verification_data: dict) -> bool: ...
    async def withdraw(self, user_id: str, consent_type: str) -> None: ...

2. Safety Engine (Gateway-Extending — adds domain-specific detection)

class GovernanceSafetyEngine(Protocol):
    """Domain-specific PII handling. Extends Gateway's generic Presidio."""
    # PROACTIVE: Detect and anonymize before LLM call
    async def detect_domain_pii(self, text: str, profile: str) -> list[PIIDetection]: ...
    async def anonymize_with_mapping(self, text: str, detections: list) -> tuple[str, str]: ...

    # REACTIVE: Restore after LLM call
    async def deanonymize(self, text: str, mapping_id: str) -> str: ...

3. Cost Engine (Gateway-Querying — queries LiteLLM, adds alerting)

class GovernanceCostEngine(Protocol):
    """Cost alerting and reporting. Queries Gateway—does NOT duplicate storage."""
    # PROACTIVE: Check budget before LLM call
    async def check_budget_status(self, tenant_id: str) -> BudgetStatus:
        # Queries LiteLLM_TeamTable
        ...
    async def check_alert_threshold(self, tenant_id: str) -> AlertStatus:
        # Compares Gateway spend against governance_alert_config
        ...

    # REACTIVE: Generate reports from Gateway data
    async def query_gateway_spend(self, tenant_id: str, date_range: DateRange) -> SpendData: ...
    async def generate_cost_report(self, tenant_id: str, regulation: str, date_range: DateRange) -> CostReport: ...

4. Audit Engine (Gateway-Querying — logs governance events, queries Gateway for unified reports)

docs.title: Governance Pipeline Runner
docs.text:
The Governance Service wraps AI operations using configured pipelines:

class GovernanceRunner:
    async def wrap(self, context: GovernanceContext, operation: Callable) -> Any:
        # 1. Run governance-specific request guards (consent, domain PII, topic)
        for guard in self.pipeline.request_guards:
            result = await guard.evaluate(context)
            if result.decision == BLOCK:
                await self.governance_audit.log_guard_decision(context, result)
                raise GovernanceBlockedError(result.reason)
            if result.decision == MODIFY:
                context.content = result.modified_content

        # 2. Check budget via gateway (LiteLLM handles enforcement)
        #    Governance adds warning alerts before hard block
        alert_status = await self.budget_checker.check_alert_threshold(context.tenant_id)
        if alert_status.should_warn:
            await self.send_budget_alert(context.tenant_id, alert_status)

        # 3. Execute operation via LLM Gateway
        #    Gateway handles: routing, failover, generic guardrails, cost tracking, logging
        result = await operation(context)

        # NOTE: Cost recording happens automatically in gateway's LiteLLM_SpendLogs
        # No need to record here - governance queries gateway for reports

        # 4. Run governance-specific response guards (PHI disclosure, minor data)
        for guard in self.pipeline.response_guards:
            guard_result = await guard.evaluate(context, result)
            if guard_result.decision == BLOCK:
                await self.governance_audit.log_guard_decision(context, guard_result)
                raise GovernanceBlockedError(guard_result.reason)
            if guard_result.decision == MODIFY:
                result.content = guard_result.modified_content

        # 5. Log governance-specific audit event (consent verified, guards passed)
        #    NOTE: LLM request/response already logged by gateway
        await self.governance_audit.log_request_completed(context)

        return result

docs.title: LLM Gateway Layer: Cross-Cutting Infrastructure for AI Governance
Executive Summary
docs.text:
The LLM Gateway Layer is a foundational infrastructure component within the Agentic Governance & Safety Framework that provides unified, abstracted access to multiple Large Language Model (LLM) providers. This layer solves critical cross-cutting concerns around provider flexibility, cost optimization, failover resilience, and operational governance—enabling organizations to swap, scale, and govern AI providers without application-level changes.

This document evaluates the Build vs Buy decision, compares leading solutions (OpenRouter vs LiteLLM), and provides a recommended architecture integrating LiteLLM as the gateway layer within the Inclusive Architecture.

docs.title: Cross-Cutting Concerns Requiring Gateway Solution
docs.text:
1. Provider Lock-In: Direct SDK integrations create tight coupling to specific providers
  2. No Fallback Strategy: Service disruptions affect availability without automatic failover
  3. Manual Cost Tracking: Token counting requires custom implementation per provider
  4. Inconsistent API Patterns: Different SDKs require different code paths for same operations
  5. Limited Model Selection: Inability to leverage best-in-class models from different providers
  6. Compliance Gaps: No unified layer for governance policies across all LLM calls

docs.title: Option A: Build — Custom Gateway
docs.text:
Approach: Develop internal abstraction layer over multiple LLM provider SDKs.

Aspect Assessment Development Effort 3-6 months for MVP, ongoing maintenance Provider Coverage Limited to prioritized providers Feature Parity Continuous catch-up with provider updates Cost Tracking Requires manual pricing table maintenance Failover Logic Custom implementation needed Maintenance Burden High — API changes, new models, pricing updates

Hidden Costs: - Continuous SDK version updates - Pricing table maintenance (changes monthly) - New model support delays - Security patching across multiple SDKs - Documentation and onboarding

Verdict: ❌ Not Recommended — High ongoing cost, diverts resources from core product development.

docs.title: Option B: Buy — LLM Gateway Solutions
docs.text: Two mature gateway solutions exist that provide unified LLM access: OpenRouter (managed SaaS) and LiteLLM (self-hosted open source).

docs.title: When to Choose Each
docs.text: Scenario Recommendation Rapid prototyping / POC OpenRouter — zero setup Non-sensitive data workloads OpenRouter — simpler Regulatory compliance (healthcare, education) LiteLLM — data residency, no third-party exposure Enterprise governance requirements LiteLLM — budget controls, guardrails Multi-tenant SaaS with billing LiteLLM — per-team cost tracking Cost optimization at scale LiteLLM — no margin, routing strategies

docs.title: Verdict
docs.text: LiteLLM is the recommended choice because: 1. Data residency — Critical for compliance needs 2. Built-in governance — Cost tracking, budgets, guardrails reduce custom implementation 3. No cost margin — Direct provider pricing at scale 4. Extensibility — Custom guardrails for PHI, domain-specific compliance
